subject: Accounting
title: Cynthia Cooper at WorldCom
description: One-minute skill: Cynthia Cooper at WorldCom.

hook.text: Cynthia Cooper worked nights and weekends in secret—digging through WorldCom's books alone.

buildup.text: As head of internal audit, she noticed suspicious capital expenditure entries that didn't add up.

discovery.text: She found that $3.8 billion in expenses had been reclassified as assets to inflate profits.

twist.text: Her own CFO ordered her to stop investigating. She refused and took findings to the audit committee.

climax.text: Her courage triggered the largest fraud investigation of its era and saved countless future victims.

punchline.text: They told her to stop. She dug deeper instead.

quiz.question: How did Cynthia Cooper respond when told to stop investigating?
options: She refused and escalated to the audit committee

details.summary: Cynthia Cooper led WorldCom's internal audit team in uncovering an $11 billion accounting fraud—one of the largest in history. This topic tells the story of her investigation and the personal risks she took to expose the truth.
details.whyItMatters: Cooper's story shows that internal auditors can be the last line of defense against fraud, even when senior management is complicit. Her courage reshaped expectations for internal audit functions.
takeaways: Cooper's team discovered WorldCom had improperly capitalized billions in expenses
She investigated at night to avoid detection by executives involved in the fraud
Her actions led to the largest bankruptcy filing in U.S. history at the time

faq.question: What did Cynthia Cooper discover at WorldCom?
faq.answer: Cooper discovered that WorldCom had fraudulently capitalized over $3.8 billion in operating expenses (later revised to $11 billion), making the company appear profitable when it was actually losing money, in one of history's largest accounting frauds.

faq.question: Why is Cynthia Cooper important in accounting history?
faq.answer: Cooper demonstrated the critical role of internal auditors as fraud detectors. Named TIME Person of the Year in 2002, her actions led to WorldCom's exposure, CEO conviction, and strengthened the case for Sarbanes-Oxley reforms.
